I started off just like you, a single system administrator, and salaried... sounds like you might be hourly considering you need to get approved for overtime, which in your case might be a good thing. Because actually, you want to avoid overtime for very basic reasons; people NEED time off, period. Also, the employer wants to reduce overtime, and they don't want to lose the sole remaining technology person.

When the stress level increases, take a break. Literally get up from what you're doing, and just walk away for a bit. I say this because I sense you're younger and prone to frustration, so just release the pressure, and come back to whatever it was you were doing, and resume. This takes practice, trust me, and it can seem awkward when it happens as the result of end-user interaction, but it must be done. Anyway, back to overtime, simply don't do it, and it's not the end of the world if some work has to wait to get finished. At this point, that is unavoidable, and you have to embrace the fact you're in a no-win situation. In a popular sci-fi series, this is called the "Kobayashi Maru," and the captain simply has to deal with the bad situation and find the best outcome. That is you right now. The best outcome is to have weekends off and let the work pile up. That work is never going to reduce; it's only going to grow, and you are one person. So let nature take its course, do the BEST you can DO, never seem to be idle... go from one task to the next, and close out tickets or whatever. Tracking your work is critical here, so you can demonstrate to your management that your productivity is peaked. This will come in handy for that conversation with management; they like to have metrics to make decisions. That is how management works; it's data-driven, so it's your responsibility to generate the data they need to do their job. That might seem cold and psychopathic, but that is the situation we all face in the IT world. Anyway, if you absolutely must perform some kind of critical off-hour work, then yes, schedule overtime, but don't ask for permission. Just do the needful, and only the needful. This comes down to defining what "critical work" means to you and your department. Not just critical stuff; you have to define the importance of every task and prioritize. Spend more time doing that, planning your work, and plotting how your time is spent. In other words, pay more focus on your workflow than the work itself. Because you are the sole system administrator, you pretty much get unilateral decision power here, so be reasonable when these choices are later questioned. This brings me to the next point: do everything out in the open and professional, because when the backlog of work begins to complain, you WILL be scrutinized, and you need to be squeaky clean in terms of work ethics and workflows.

Trust me, when you implement these ideas, your frustration just fizzles away. Consider that people working in a fast-food restaurant have the same exact problems you have. Service desk and system administrator work are not very different from the fast-food industry if you think about it. You're providing a service to customers, and you really have to be polite and courteous despite the challenges. Your managers are probably not very experienced; they are in an academic institution, so they probably don't have industry experience, and believe me, managing people like yourself (like most IT people in general) is not exactly easy. So keep that in perspective; they are inexperienced, and IT folks are not easy to manage.

So when your day ends, leave. When your weekend comes, do something for yourself, and forget about work. When Monday comes, be refreshed and ready to excel. You will be way more productive if you have these boundaries set, and probably management will eventually be forced to hire another employee to help you. Meanwhile, you will gain valuable experience that you can apply to your next IT job.
